modules.name: Louis Pasteur
modules.outcome: Explain, from Pasteur's own experiments, why dust, hands and tools carry microbes to food and why heat, covers and clean handling work, and design a handling routine for a kitchen with no running water.
modules.intro: Louis Pasteur did not argue that germs were in the air. He collected them, counted what survived, and found the hidden source of error in other people's experiments. His 1864 address is a method for finding where contamination comes from.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read his 1864 Sorbonne address in an English translation, in full. It is Pasteur's own account, delivered to a public audience, so the record is rich for these experiments. {{pasteur-1864}} The Institut Pasteur and Britannica pages are secondary summaries. {{inst-pasteur}} {{brit-pasteur}}
The translation uses the old phrase Arctic Sea for what the French calls the Mer de Glace glacier on Mont Blanc. We keep his figures and note this. {{pasteur-1864}}
His method, step by step

i: Treat it as a question of fact. He says the question of spontaneous generation is a matter of fact, to be addressed without prejudice, and that he would declare for spontaneous generation if experiment attested it. {{pasteur-1864}}

Show that dust carries living things. He draws air through a glass tube with a wad of cotton in one end, which keeps nearly all the dust, washes the cotton in a little water, and puts the droplets on a slide. Under the microscope, among soot and fragments of cloth, are organised corpuscles that cannot be told apart from mould seeds. {{pasteur-1864}}

Test that the dust, not the air, is the cause. He burns air-borne particles collected on an asbestos pad in a flame and seeds a vial with them. The infusion stays intact, as if never seeded. {{pasteur-1864}}

Control the heat and the path. He boils an infusion in a flask with a long neck bent and stretched over a torch, left open to the air. It stays unaltered for months and, at the time of the address, years, while the same infusion in a straight-necked flask is altered in days. {{pasteur-1864}}

Explain the difference. Everything in the air except dust enters the curved flask easily. The dust falls on the curved neck. If the flask is shaken, so that air enters fast and brings the liquid into contact with dust, the infusion is altered two or three days later. {{pasteur-1864}}

Find the hidden source of error. He shows that a vat of mercury, used in an opponent's experiment, carries dust into the flask whenever anything is dipped through it. The experiment was beyond reproach for the factors the author had watched, but not for this one. {{pasteur-1864}}

blocks.x: He also notes that the dust in a room can carry sickness or death, in the form of typhus, cholera, yellow fever and other fluxes. {{pasteur-1864}}

The Institut Pasteur says his 1862 conclusions were that airborne dust contains microorganisms that develop and multiply, and that microbes are found in water, in air, on objects and on the skin. {{inst-pasteur}}

Pasteur's experiments are about liquids held clear of dust. A real kitchen is not a laboratory, and a rule such as keep it covered does not make food safe by itself. Use his findings for where contamination comes from and how to block it, and use your course's tested temperatures and times for the rest. {{pasteur-1864}}

blocks.title: How exposed air changes the odds
steps: He opened sealed vials of a clear, perishable infusion in different places and reseal them. At the glacier, 19 of 20 stayed intact. In the Jura mountains, 15 of 20. At the foot of the Jura, 12 of 20. {{pasteur-1864}}
Convert to the share altered: 1 of 20 is 5 percent, 5 of 20 is 25 percent, and 8 of 20 is 40 percent.
The altered share at the lowest place is 8 times that at the glacier (40 ÷ 5). Where the air carries more dust, more flasks spoil. {{pasteur-1864}}
One night in a room at the inn gave 10 altered of 30, which is 33 percent. {{pasteur-1864}}
The lesson for a kitchen is not these numbers. It is that spoilage is a matter of how much dust, and so how many germs, reach the food, so the fewer routes in, the fewer losses.

blocks.x: Apply it: a clean-handling routine for a dry tap

i: Assume everything you touch may carry microbes, including hands, boards and cloths.
Set up a hand-cleaning step before food: sanitiser, or a small measured amount of safe water and soap, and dry on a clean cloth.
Cover food and water between uses. Move cloths and bedding away from the food area.
Use one clean board and knife for ready-to-eat food and another for raw food.
Heat food to the temperature your course gives, and write it down.

blocks.x: Write a clean-handling routine for your kitchen. Mark each step with which of Pasteur's routes it blocks: dust, hands, tools or heat.

blocks.q: What did Pasteur find in the cotton wad after dust was drawn through it?
o: Organised corpuscles like mould seeds among the soot and fibres
blocks.w: Among the amorphous objects he found organised corpuscles that looked like mould seeds. {{pasteur-1864}}

blocks.q: Why did the long-necked open flask stay clear?
o: Dust fell on the curved neck before reaching the broth
blocks.w: The dust falls on the curved neck before reaching the liquid. {{pasteur-1864}}

blocks.q: What was the hidden source of error in Pouchet's experiment?
o: The vat of mercury, which carried dust into the flask
blocks.w: He showed that the mercury vat introduces dust. {{pasteur-1864}}

i: Contamination arrives on dust, hands and tools. {{pasteur-1864}}
Heat and a covered path block it. {{pasteur-1864}}
Look for the hidden route, as he did with the mercury vat. {{pasteur-1864}}

quiz.q: What did Pasteur's swan-neck flask show about boiled broth kept from fresh air?
quiz.w: The liquid stayed unaltered because dust could not reach it. {{pasteur-1864}} {{brit-pasteur}}

modules.name: Louis Pasteur
modules.outcome: Use Pasteur's observations on how fast and how often perishable liquids spoil to order food by risk in the first hours of a power cut, and say what heating does and does not do.
modules.intro: Pasteur's address and his work on wine give three practical facts: warm perishable food spoils within a day, exposure to more dust spoils more, and heating helps but has limits.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read his 1864 address in full, and Britannica and Institut Pasteur summaries. His address gives the observations on timing and exposure. The pasteurisation figures are from Britannica, not from the address. {{pasteur-1864}} {{brit-pasteurization}} {{inst-pasteur}}
His method, step by step

i: Use a perishable test liquid and watch it. He describes a clear infusion so sensitive that, at a temperature between 15 and 25 degrees, it would be completely clouded the next day. {{pasteur-1864}}
Keep the conditions the same and vary one thing. He opened twenty sealed vials of the same infusion in each place and counted how many altered. {{pasteur-1864}}
Count, do not guess. In one place 19 of 20 stayed clear, in another 15 of 20, in a third 12 of 20, and after a night in an inn room 10 of 30 altered. {{pasteur-1864}}

Remove the cause without heat to see it is the cause. Blood and urine drawn by a special technique from living, healthy animals and exposed only to air from which the dust and germs were removed stayed unaltered, never having been heated, since March 1863. {{pasteur-1864}}
Apply heat to keep, within limits. Britannica says Pasteur's heating of wine and beer used about 57 degrees Celsius for a few minutes to prevent abnormal fermentation. {{brit-pasteurization}}
Know what heat does not do. Pasteurisation does not destroy all microbes or their spores, so heated food is not safe for ever. {{brit-pasteurization}}

blocks.x: Pasteur worked in glass vials with a clear infusion. Food is lumpier and richer than an infusion, and some foods spoil more dangerously than they look. This lesson uses his observations to rank risks, and your course's tested times and temperatures decide what is safe to eat. {{pasteur-1864}}

steps: List what is in the fridge and freezer. Mark each as perishable (cooked meat, dairy, cut fruit) or stable (hard cheese, whole fruit, vegetables with skins).
Pasteur's sensitive infusion clouded within a day at room temperature, so rank by how much a microbe has to feed on and how recently it was cooked or opened. {{pasteur-1864}}

Put the cooked and opened items first. If the power is off for 4 hours, check the fridge thermometer reading against your course's limit and apply it. The limit comes from your food-safety source, not from Pasteur.
Keep the freezer shut. Eat what you can from the fridge before opening the freezer.
Write the order on a card on the fridge door, with the time the power went off.

Use your course's safe temperature limits to decide eat, cook or discard.
Write the time the power went off, and the time each decision was made.

modules.name: John Snow
modules.outcome: Design a comparison of two groups that differ in one thing, check your data the way Snow did, report the result with its numbers, and say when new data changes the answer.
modules.intro: John Snow found cholera's link to a water supply by comparing two groups of houses that differed only in who supplied the water. His account also shows him correcting his own ratio when better data came in.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read Snow's own paper Cholera and the Water Supply in the South Districts of London in 1854 in full. It is the primary source, so the record is rich. The 315 and 37 per 10,000 figures come from a secondary table read in an earlier pass. {{snow-water}} {{snow-ije}}
The Broad Street pump story is a different Snow study and is not in this paper. We did not read it in this pass. {{wiki-broad}}
His method, step by step

i: Notice a difference in outcome. When cholera returned in 1854, he saw the same advantage for districts partly supplied from Thames Ditton as in the earlier epidemic. {{snow-water}}

Look for a natural experiment. The pipes of the two water companies went down the same streets and into nearly all the courts and alleys, so a single house often had a different supply from its neighbours. {{snow-water}}

Check that the groups are comparable. Each company supplied rich and poor alike, so a population of about 300,000 people of various conditions and occupations was divided into two groups by no other circumstance than the water. {{snow-water}}

Collect the data house by house. He made the supply of each fatal case a matter of personal inquiry, and did not rely on the resident's reply or the look of the water, but asked for the receipt for the water rate. {{snow-water}}
Add a second check. A chemical test of the water helped, since a mixture of sea water extended further up the Thames than usual in the dry weather. {{snow-water}}

Report the numbers and what they mean. In the first four weeks, 9 July to 5 August, there were 334 deaths, of which 286 were in houses supplied by the Southwark and Vauxhall Company and 14 in houses supplied by the Lambeth Company. {{snow-water}}

blocks.x: Of the remaining deaths, 4 were from a pump well, 26 from water drawn directly from the river, a canal or a tidal ditch, and 4 had no supply ascertained. {{snow-water}}

He gives the rates: the Southwark and Vauxhall Company supplied 40,046 houses with an estimated 266,516 people, and the Lambeth Company 26,107 houses with 173,748 people, so the mortality was 107 per 100,000 for the first and 8 per 100,000 for the second. {{snow-water}}

He also shows that more data changed his figure. A supplemental inquiry showed 125 and 37 per 10,000 for the two companies, a difference of 3½ to 1, instead of 160 and 27, a difference of 6 to 1. He argues even the smaller difference does not explain the variation across districts. {{snow-water}}

Snow's early ratio is not the same across his reports, because the data changed as he collected more. A good comparison states which figure it is quoting and from which weeks. The 315 and 37 per 10,000 houses figure in some secondary tables is for a different measure and period. {{snow-water}} {{snow-ije}}

blocks.title: Checking Snow's numbers
steps: The Southwark and Vauxhall rate is 286 deaths ÷ 266,516 people = 0.001073, which is 107 per 100,000. {{snow-water}}
The Lambeth rate is 14 ÷ 173,748 = 0.0000806, which is 8 per 100,000. {{snow-water}}
The ratio of the rates is 107 ÷ 8, about 13 to 1.
Compare with his later supplemental figure of 3½ to 1 for a longer period and larger area. The ratio depends on the weeks and the data, so quote the figure with its period. {{snow-water}}

Now do your own: if 4 of 20 people who ate dish A fell ill and 1 of 20 who did not eat it fell ill, the rates are 20 percent and 5 percent, a ratio of 4 to 1. Ask what else the two groups differ in before you blame the dish.

blocks.x: Apply it: a two-group comparison for a household

i: Write where each person gets water or food: tap, stored container, shop-bought, river or well.
If two people fall ill, ask what they ate and drank, and whether the source differs from those who stayed well.
Check that the groups are alike in other ways (age, who prepared the food).
Verify the source with evidence, such as a receipt or a test, not just a reply.
Write rates with the numerator and denominator, not just 'most'.

blocks.x: Write a water or food log for one week. If anyone falls ill, work out the rates for the people who did and did not share each source.

o: The two companies' pipes ran side by side, so neighbours differed only in supply
blocks.w: A single house often had a different supply from either neighbour. {{snow-water}}

blocks.q: How did he check each house's supply?
o: He asked for the water-rate receipt and used a chemical test
blocks.w: He did not rest content with the reply and asked for the receipt, helped by a chemical test. {{snow-water}}

blocks.q: Why quote the weeks with a ratio?
o: The ratio changed as he gathered more data
It is a rule of grammar
blocks.w: His ratio changed from 6 to 1 to 3½ to 1 with more data. {{snow-water}}

i: Compare groups that differ in one thing. {{snow-water}}
Verify each case with evidence, not the reply. {{snow-water}}
State the figures with their weeks, and revise when data changes.

quiz.w: The secondary table gives 315 per 10,000 houses, from a different measure than the first-four-weeks rate. {{snow-ije}}

modules.name: Count Rumford (Benjamin Thompson)
modules.outcome: Cost a bulk meal in ingredients, fuel and labour, cook it with controlled heat, and use stored heat to cut fuel use when fuel is scarce.
modules.intro: Count Rumford fed 1,200 people a day at the Munich House of Industry on one costed recipe and wrote down every price. His essay shows that for a well-run pot the fuel was the smallest line on the bill, and that a covered boiler can finish a soup on stored heat.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read Essay III of his Essays, Political, Economical, and Philosophical (Volume 1), including the soup recipe, the method and the costed table. This is Rumford's own account, so the record is rich for these claims. {{rumford-essays}}

The fuel-saving principles about covers and regulating the draught come from a Victorian summary of his work, which we read in an earlier pass. We did not read his fuel essay, which is in a later volume. {{rumford-psm}}
His method, step by step

i: Start from the need and the price. He writes that necessity is the mother of invention, and says the high price of corn had turned attention to the science of nutrition. {{rumford-essays}}

Find the cheapest nourishing food by trial. After experiments he found the cheapest, most savoury and most nourishing food to be a soup of pearl barley, peas, potatoes, cuttings of fine wheaten bread, vinegar, salt and water in set proportions. {{rumford-essays}}

Cook in a set order. The water and barley boil first, the peas are added and the boiling continued over a gentle fire for about two hours, the potatoes are added for about one hour more, the soup is stirred to a uniform mass, then vinegar and salt, and last the bread cuttings at the moment of serving. {{rumford-essays}}
Do not overcook the late additions. The soup should never be suffered to boil, or even stand long, after the bread is put in, and the bread is best put into the serving tubs. {{rumford-essays}}

Cost every line. He lists weights and costs of each ingredient, the fuel, the cooks' wages and food, the servants and the repairs, and gives a total daily expense for feeding 1,200 people. {{rumford-essays}}

Use stored heat. He says the soup is improved if a small fire is made just enough to boil the barley and water once, the ash-hole register and the chimney damper are closed, and a thick blanket is thrown over the boiler cover so the contents stay hot until the next morning. {{rumford-essays}}

blocks.x: A Victorian summary of his principles says every boiler and stew-pan should have a cover to confine the heat, and each fireplace should let the cook regulate the air, so that the rate of burning can be controlled. {{rumford-psm}}
Wikipedia says the soup used pearl barley, dried peas, potatoes and sour beer, slowly boiled until thick, and was a cheap, filling ration cooked in bulk. {{wiki-rsoup}}

Rumford's kitchen was a purpose-built set of boilers in a brick kitchen, fed with dry pine wood. A camp stove or a fire in a grate is different, and a boiler wrapped in a blanket is not a safe way to hold food at a warm temperature for many hours. For food safety, use your course's rules on keeping food hot or cooling it, and use his hot-hold idea only with the time and temperature checks this course gives. {{rumford-essays}}

blocks.x: Worked example: checking his per-portion cost and fuel share (his figures, our arithmetic)

blocks.title: Is fuel the cost to worry about?
steps: £1 15s 2¼d is 240 + 180 + 2.25 = 422.25 pence, as £1 is 240 pence and 1s is 12 pence. {{rumford-essays}}
Divided by 1,200 portions, that is 422.25 ÷ 1,200 = 0.352 pence, a trifle more than a third of a penny, as he says. {{rumford-essays}}
The fuel, 2¼d, is 2.25 ÷ 422.25 = 0.53 percent of the day's cost. In weight, 88 lb of wood to 1,485 lb 10 oz of soup is 5.9 percent. {{rumford-essays}}

So in his kitchen the money went into food and labour, and a good pot made the fuel line small. In your kitchen the fuel is scarce, so it matters more, but his lesson is to measure it rather than assume.
Do the same for one pot: write the cost or weight of ingredients, fuel and your time for one meal, and see which line is largest.

blocks.x: Apply it: a one-pot, low-fuel plan

i: List what you must cook today and how many people you feed.
Choose one lidded pot. Bring it to the boil, then lower the heat and keep it covered.
Order the ingredients by cooking time, as he did: slow items first, quick items last, delicate items at the end.
If your course allows it, test a stored-heat finish with a well-insulated pot and check the food temperature with a thermometer before you eat or hold it.
Weigh the fuel before and after and cost the meal in ingredients, fuel and time.

quiz.q: Which is a Rumford-style way to save fuel?
o: Use a covered pot and control the heat
quiz.w: Covers confine the heat, and controlling the burn saves fuel. {{rumford-psm}}

modules.name: Nicolas Appert
modules.outcome: Describe Appert's four-step process, explain why a method that worked by trial still needs tested times today, and judge a preserving source by whether it gives your food, jar and time.
modules.intro: Nicolas Appert preserved food in sealed glass bottles heated in water, with no theory of why it worked. His own book shows careful steps, honest losses and a clear statement of what he did not know.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read the opening sections of his book in the 1812 English edition, including the four steps, the vessels, corking and his experiments. It is his own account, so the record is rich for the method. {{appert-1812}} Britannica gives the background. {{brit-appert}} {{brit-canning}}
His method, step by step

i: Name the problem with the old methods. He says all earlier expedients reduce to two: drying, and mixing in a foreign substance to impede fermentation or putrefaction, and that each has its inconveniences. Drying takes away odour and changes taste, and sugar conceals other flavours. {{appert-1812}}

State the process in four steps: enclose the substance in bottles, cork the bottles with the utmost care because success chiefly depends on the corking, submit the bottles to boiling water in a water bath for a time that depends on the substance, and withdraw them at the right time. {{appert-1812}}

State the principle. The principle by which substances are preserved is invariable in its effects. The result in each experiment depends on how well the principle is applied to the particular substance, and the exclusion of air is a precaution of the utmost importance. {{appert-1812}}

Choose the container for the job. He chose glass as the matter most impenetrable by air, and made his bottles with stronger, better-formed necks, since ordinary bottles were too weak for the blows of the bat and the heat. {{appert-1812}}
Leave room. He fills liquid bottles to within three inches of the rim and vegetable and fruit bottles to within two inches, lest they burst from the bubbling and swelling in the heat. {{appert-1812}}

Explain failure honestly. He says losses had no other cause than an erroneous application of the principle or some negligence or omission in the preparation, and that a defect in a vessel or in the interior of a cork may spoil the contents. {{appert-1812}}

blocks.x: He gives examples of times. Beef and fowl in a water bath were kept at the boil for two hours, and milk in its bottle for two hours. He stores finished bottles on shelves in a cool, shady place, and reports having bottles lying three years under a staircase with the contents sound. {{appert-1812}}

A letter from the French Minister of the Interior dated 30 January 1810 says the Board of Arts and Manufactures had examined the process and that no doubt could be entertained of its success. It adds that preserving food could be of the utmost utility in sea voyages, in hospitals and in domestic economy. {{appert-1812}}

Britannica says the French government offered a prize in 1795 for a way to conserve food for transport, and that Pasteur later explained that the heat killed microorganisms and the seal stopped new ones entering. {{brit-appert}} {{brit-canning}}

Appert's explanation was the exclusion of air. Pasteur's work half a century later showed that the cause was germs, which is why the heat and the seal both mattered. A method that works by trial can fail in a new setting, for example with a different food or a larger jar. {{appert-1812}} {{brit-canning}}

This lesson does not give canning times. Safe times and temperatures depend on the food, the jar size and the method, and low-acid foods carry serious risks that Appert did not know about. Use a current tested source from a food-safety agency for any home preserving. This is our safety advice and is not in Appert's text.

steps: The card says: fill jars, boil 20 minutes, done. Check it against Appert's own standard of a time that depends on the substance. {{appert-1812}}
Does it say which food, which jar size and how full? Appert fills bottles to a stated distance below the rim and times by substance. {{appert-1812}}
Does it come from a tested source, with times for your jar and food? If not, do not rely on it, because Appert's trial method only worked in his conditions.
Does it say why it works? Modern guidance relies on the science of germs that Pasteur supplied. {{brit-canning}}
If any answer is no, do not use the card. Use a tested source from a food-safety agency.

blocks.x: Apply it: a checklist for any preserving method

i: Is the method from a tested source, with times for your exact food, jar size and fill level?
Does the source say why it works, and what the limits are?
Is the seal checked, and the storage stated?
Are the risks for your food type (for example low-acid foods) stated and followed?
If you cannot answer all four, do not use the method for food others will eat.

blocks.x: Take one preserving recipe you have seen and test it against the four checklist questions. Write what is missing.

blocks.q: According to Appert, on what did success chiefly depend?
blocks.w: He says it is chiefly on the corking that success depends. {{appert-1812}}

blocks.q: Why did he leave two or three inches below the rim?
o: So the bottles would not burst from bubbling and swelling in the heat
blocks.w: He left room lest they burst. {{appert-1812}}

blocks.q: Who later explained why the sealed, heated bottles kept the food?
blocks.w: Britannica says Pasteur later explained that the heat killed microorganisms and the seal stopped new ones. {{brit-canning}}

i: The method worked before the reason was known. {{appert-1812}}
Time depends on the substance, so use tested times for your food. {{appert-1812}}
Never trust a preserving card that does not say what and how long.

quiz.q: Who later explained why Appert's sealed and heated jars kept food?
quiz.w: Britannica says Pasteur later explained that the heat killed microorganisms and the seal stopped new ones entering. {{brit-canning}}

modules.name: Benjamin Franklin
modules.outcome: Write short rules, assign roles, set a drill timetable and a debrief for a household food plan, in the way Franklin proposed for fire.
modules.intro: Benjamin Franklin's 1735 letter on fire starts from prevention, names exact hazards, proposes licensing and fines so someone is accountable, and ends with a society of people who drill and meet to learn from fires. It is a template for a household plan.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson

We read his letter On Protection of Towns from Fire (1735) in full from the Founders Online edition, and a page on the Union Fire Company. His letter is a primary source and the record is rich. {{franklin-fire}} {{ush-fire}}
His method, step by step

i: Start with prevention. As an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, he advises not carrying live brand-ends or coals in an open shovel from room to room, because scraps of fire may fall into chinks and show nothing until midnight. {{franklin-fire}}
Name the exact hazards. Shallow hearths, and wooden mouldings by the fireplace made of heart-of-pine full of turpentine, ready to flame at a coal. {{franklin-fire}}

Make someone accountable. Anyone could sweep chimneys, and if one fired through the sweeper's fault the owner paid the fine. He says sweepers should be licensed, and fined if a chimney fires within 15 days of sweeping. {{franklin-fire}}
Check the supply. He doubts there is water enough in many parts of the town to keep the engines going half an hour and suggests public pumps. {{franklin-fire}}

Add order and method. The town does not want for hands or goodwill but seems to want order and method. He offers the example of a society of active men attached to each engine, who attend all fires and work the engine once a quarter. {{franklin-fire}}

Give roles and authority. Some handle the firehooks and others the axes, and officers called firewards, with red staffs, direct the opening of roofs, the pulling down of burning timbers and the removal of goods, with fines for disobedience. {{franklin-fire}}

blocks.x: At their quarterly meetings the officers and the men discuss fires, the faults at some and the good management at others, and so, by communicating their thoughts and experience, grow wise in the thing. {{franklin-fire}}

He warns that the town has been lucky: the bad circumstances of a dry season, high wind, narrow streets and little water have never all come together, which makes people feel secure. {{franklin-fire}}
On 7 December 1736 about thirty men formed the Union Fire Company, brought leather buckets to every fire, and met monthly to talk about fire prevention and fighting. {{ush-fire}}
Some of Franklin's proposals involve fines and imprisonment under law. A household cannot fine anyone, so the household version is agreed rules and roles, a drill and a debrief. {{franklin-fire}}

blocks.x: Worked example: a one-page rule set and drill timetable (illustrative)

blocks.title: A four-person household
steps: Write five short rules that decide most cases fast. For example: the fridge door stays shut; cooked food is eaten first; nothing is eaten that has been in the danger zone longer than the course's limit; hands are cleaned before food; the record-keeper writes every decision with a time.
Give each person one role: water, cold store, cooking, records. If someone is away, the next person takes the role.

Franklin's society worked the engine once a quarter, which is 4 times a year. {{franklin-fire}} The Union Fire Company met monthly, 12 times a year. {{ush-fire}} Choose your drill rhythm: with 4 drills a year, each person practises each role about once a year if you rotate roles.
After each drill, hold a 10-minute debrief: one fault, one thing that went well, one change to the rules. {{franklin-fire}}
Keep the rules to one page and put it on the fridge.

blocks.x: Apply it: rules, roles, drill, debrief

i: Write five rules in short sentences that decide most cases fast.
Assign a named person to each role and a deputy for each.
Set a date for the first drill and agree what you will test.
Run the drill with the power off for an hour. Time each task.
Hold the debrief at once. Write one change to the rules, and date it.

blocks.x: Write a one-page rule set, assign the roles and schedule the first drill and debrief.

blocks.q: What did Franklin say the town lacked in fighting fires?
blocks.w: He says they did not want hands or goodwill but seemed to want order and method. {{franklin-fire}}

blocks.q: How often did the engine societies work their engines, in his proposal?
blocks.w: They worked it once a quarter and kept it in order. {{franklin-fire}}

blocks.q: Why did the officers hold quarterly meetings?
o: To discuss faults and good management and learn from experience
blocks.w: They discourse of fires, of the faults and the good management, and grow wise. {{franklin-fire}}

i: Prevention, then roles, drills and a debrief. {{franklin-fire}}
Short rules and named roles decide fast under stress. {{franklin-fire}}
Practise before the emergency. {{ush-fire}}

quiz.q: Which habit from Franklin's fire company suits a household food plan?
quiz.w: Agreed roles, regular meetings and practice. {{franklin-fire}} {{ush-fire}}

modules.name: Benjamin Franklin
modules.outcome: Score your 72-hour plan on a daily check grid, using short precepts and one habit at a time, in the style of Franklin's virtues chart.
modules.intro: Franklin found that knowing what was right was not enough to do it, so he built a method: short precepts, one habit at a time, and a daily mark for each lapse. The same grid scores a three-day food plan.

blocks.x: The record behind this lesson
We read page 38 of his Autobiography in full from a history site. It is his own account of the method, so the record is rich for the chart. {{franklin-auto}}
His method, step by step

i: Admit the gap between knowing and doing. He found the mere speculative conviction that it was our interest to be virtuous was not sufficient to prevent slipping, and concluded that the contrary habits must be broken and good ones acquired and established. {{franklin-auto}}
Use more names with fewer ideas each. For the sake of clearness he used thirteen names of virtues, each with a short precept that fully expressed the extent he gave to it. {{franklin-auto}}

Write the precept in one line. Examples from his list: Order, Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time. Cleanliness, Tolerate no uncleanliness in body, clothes, or habitation. {{franklin-auto}}
Take one at a time. He judged it best not to attempt the whole at once but to fix his attention on one virtue at a time and, when master of that, to proceed to the next. {{franklin-auto}}
Arrange them in an order that helps. As the acquisition of some might facilitate the acquisition of others, he arranged them with that view, with Temperance first. {{franklin-auto}}

Examine daily. He made a little book with a page for each virtue, ruled with seven columns for the days of the week and thirteen lines for the virtues, and marked a black spot for every fault found that day. {{franklin-auto}}

blocks.title: A check grid for a 72-hour plan (the left column is our adaptation of his method)
head: Habit (a short precept)
Day 1
Day 2
Day 3
rows: Cold chain: eat cooked food first and keep the fridge shut
Water: safe water measured and treated
Cleanliness: hands cleaned before food
Heat: food heated to the course's temperature and noted
Records: every decision written with a time
blocks.src: Habits are our adaptation. The grid and the black spot for each lapse follow {{franklin-auto}}.

blocks.x: Worked example: reading the grid after a practice run (illustrative)

blocks.title: Scoring three days
steps: Mark a black spot for each lapse found at the end of the day, as he did. {{franklin-auto}}

Suppose day 1 has 4 spots, day 2 has 2 and day 3 has 1. The total is 7 spots over 15 habit-days (5 habits × 3 days), so the lapse rate is 7 ÷ 15 = 47 percent, falling from 80 percent (4 of 5) to 40 percent (2 of 5) to 20 percent (1 of 5).
Look by row. If Records has a spot every day and Cold chain has none, fix Records first, as he fixed one habit at a time. {{franklin-auto}}
Write one change to the plan for that row and run the grid again.
The numbers are illustrative. Keep your own marks and compare day by day.

blocks.x: Apply it: score the 72-hour plan

i: List the plan's habits in rows and write a one-line precept for each.
Run a practice run of three days, or a weekend.
At the end of each day, mark a spot for each lapse.
Pick the habit with the most spots and change the plan for it, one habit at a time.
Write a short review: three things to keep, three to change, and the next date to run the grid.

blocks.x: Make the grid for your plan, run it for three days and write the review.

blocks.q: In Franklin's chart, what did a black spot mean?
o: A fault found on that day
blocks.w: Each spot marked a fault found upon examination that day. {{franklin-auto}}

blocks.q: Why did he give each virtue a short precept?
o: To state clearly the extent he gave to its meaning
blocks.w: He annexed to each a short precept that fully expressed the extent he gave to its meaning. {{franklin-auto}}

blocks.q: How many virtues did he work on at once?
blocks.w: He fixed his attention on one at a time. {{franklin-auto}}

i: Short precepts, one habit at a time. {{franklin-auto}}
Mark each lapse daily. {{franklin-auto}}
Change one habit, then run the grid again.

quiz.q: In Franklin's chart, what did a black spot mean?
o: A fault found on that day
quiz.w: Each spot marked a fault found upon examination that day. {{franklin-auto}}
